chunks: From him, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Yasin al-Darir, from Hariz, from one who narrated to him, from Sulayman ibn Khalid, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

I asked him about a slave who wished to buy his own freedom, and a man made a gift (dass) to him. Is it permissible for the gifted one to buy the entire freedom from the slave's wealth? He said: 'If he wishes to buy the entire freedom from the slave's wealth, it is not proper. And if he wishes to make that permissible between himself and Allah, Exalted and Mighty, so that the manumission right (walā') belongs to him, then he should add from his own wealth to the price a certain amount, whether he wishes a dirham or whatever he wishes, after there is an addition from his wealth to the slave's price by which he makes the manumission right permissible, so that the slave's manumission right becomes his. And we were informed of that from Burayd.'

key_terms.الْوَلَاءُ: Manumission right (the right of the master to the freed slave's lineage/inheritance)
key_terms.لِلْمَدْسُوسِ: For the one who received the gift

ai.seo_question: What is the proper way for a slave to use gifted money to buy their freedom according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the fiqh of *kitabah* (self-purchase) by addressing the validity of a third party gifting funds to a slave. Imam al-Sadiq (AS) distinguishes between a direct gift, which may not fully transfer the *walā'* (manumission right) to the donor, and a structured transaction where the slave adds his own capital to 'purchase' the *walā'* from the donor, ensuring the legal bond of manumission is properly established. This ruling highlights the Shia scholarly emphasis on the precise transfer of rights (*walā'*) in manumission contracts, ensuring the donor retains the spiritual and social benefits of freeing the slave.
